public_rationale: This line is a rhetorical judgment, not a checkable fact. 'Most expensive scientific experiments in history' treats corporate AI build-outs as experiments but sets no cost basis to rank them by. 'Money down the drain' is a verdict on waste with no measure or time frame. The facts behind it are real. Meta spent $72.22 billion on capex in 2025 (e1). Musk said xAI was 'not built right' (e2). Meta's Avocado model fell short of rivals in internal tests (e3). But company-wide capex is not the cost of one experiment. The chips and data centers are still in use. And in April 2026, Meta's spending produced Muse Spark, reported as 'competitive but not dominant' (e4). Ruling the money wasted or not would mean choosing a definition the speaker never gave. So the claim cannot be fairly graded either way.
limitations: Meta's capex covers its core business as well as AI, so it cannot be assigned to one 'experiment'.
No xAI spending figure was confirmed from a source that could be read.
Whether AI spending pays off may take years to judge.

from_speaker: Two of the most expensive scientific experiments in history
Sooo much money down the drain
expensive experiments from two of the world's wealthiest men
Meta's latest model ... good but not great
xAI 'not built right first time around'
our_interpretation: The 'experiments' are Meta's and xAI's efforts to reach frontier AI mainly by scaling compute and data. The post does not say which costs count: the training of one model, AI capex, talent, or whole data-center build-outs.

'Most expensive scientific experiments in history' is a rhetorical comparison. It treats corporate product and infrastructure spending as a 'scientific experiment' and sets no cost figure or comparison list.

'Money down the drain' is a value judgment. It says the spending was wasted, but gives no test, time frame, or measure of return. Data centers, chips, and models keep running and earning after one model release disappoints, so 'wasted' has no plain reading that can be checked.
Reading this as a firm factual claim would require choosing a cost basis and a definition of waste that the speaker did not give. The result would then depend on the evaluator's choice.
criteria.support_condition: It would hold if an agreed cost for each effort ranked it among history's costliest science projects (e.g. Apollo, ISS, LHC, ITER), and if the spending clearly produced no lasting value: for example, assets written off, models abandoned, or programs shut down.
criteria.contradiction_condition: It would fail if the attributable costs were well below those of major science projects, or if the spending clearly produced lasting value, such as competitive models, infrastructure in use, and revenue.

evidence.excerpt:
Capital expenditures, including principal payments on nance leases, were $22.14
billion and $72.22 billion for the fourth quarter and full year 2025, respectively.
evidence.locator: Fourth Quarter and Full Year 2025 Financial Highlights, Capital expenditures paragraph
evidence.explanation: Meta's 2025 capex was very large. But it is company-wide capex, not the cost of one model 'experiment', and it says nothing about whether the money was wasted.

evidence.excerpt: “xAI was not built right first time around, so is being rebuilt from the foundations up,” Musk said Thursday on his social media platform, X.
evidence.explanation: Confirms the Musk statement the post relies on. It is an organizational admission, not a cost figure or a finding that the spending was lost.

evidence.excerpt: In internal tests, Avocado fell short of leading models from Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic in logical reasoning, programming, and writing.
evidence.explanation: Supports the post's premise that Meta's model was 'good but not great' at the time of the post. It does not measure cost or waste.

evidence.excerpt: The benchmark results published alongside the launch paint a picture of a model that is competitive but not dominant.
evidence.explanation: Within a month of the post, Meta's spending produced a model reported as competitive. That weighs against a plain 'money down the drain' reading, but whether the cost was worth it remains a judgment.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: A version of the claim with a defined cost basis and a test for waste would be checkable. For example: a stated cost of a named training program compared with named science projects, plus evidence that the resulting assets were written off or abandoned.
